scope: Thematic collections that span dynasties and centuries — the cross-cutting groupings that don't fit any single events_*.json file.

collections.title: Founding moments of modern India
collections.subtitle: From the 1857 rebellion to the Constitution — the arc by which a subcontinent of subjects became a nation.
collections.summary: 1857 was the first rebellion in which Indians from the Doab to the Deccan recognised themselves as a single political 'we'. The Crown takeover of 1858 institutionalised the Raj that the rebellion had ended in fact; the next nine decades — Indian Councils Acts, Congress, Jallianwala, Round Tables, Cabinet Mission, Independence — built the constitutional and political body of modern India, completed in the Constitution of 1950.

collections.title: European arrival on the subcontinent
collections.subtitle: Portuguese, Dutch, English, French, Danish — the trading-post network that became the imperial contest.
collections.summary: Five European maritime powers reached the Indian coast within 125 years of Vasco da Gama's 1498 Calicut landing. The pattern was the same — factory, then fort, then territory — but the political outcomes diverged sharply: Portuguese Goa held 451 years, Danish Tranquebar 225, French Pondicherry 280, Dutch Coromandel 200, the EIC's English presence one which by 1858 had become the Crown's.

collections.title: EIC ascent — from trader to sovereign
collections.subtitle: Bombay 1661 to the Doctrine of Lapse — how a trading company became a continental state.
collections.summary: The English East India Company, granted its royal charter in 1600, was for its first century one of several European trading companies on the Indian coast. The arc from Bombay-as-Catherine's-dowry through Plassey, Buxar, the Permanent Settlement, the Anglo-Mysore and Anglo-Maratha closures, and the Doctrine of Lapse annexations is the story of how that trader became, by 1856, the paramount power of the subcontinent — and triggered, in 1857, the rebellion that ended it as an institution.

collections.title: Wars of empire on Indian soil
collections.subtitle: Plassey to Mandalay — the set-piece battles that built (and lost) British India.
collections.summary: From Plassey 1757 through the Anglo-Mysore, Anglo-Maratha, Anglo-Sikh, Anglo-Burmese, and Anglo-Afghan wars, the EIC and Crown converted commercial presence into continental sovereignty by force. The First Anglo-Afghan War's catastrophic Kabul retreat 1842 was the limit case; Mandalay 1885 the closing campaign.

collections.title: Famines on the subcontinent
collections.subtitle: From Tughluq's Doab famine (1335–42) to Bengal 1943 — six centuries of monsoon-driven mortality.
collections.summary: Famines were endemic on the subcontinent across the Sultanate, Mughal, and colonial centuries — and ended, in their catastrophic form, only with the Republic. The eight events here run from the Tughluq Doab famine c. 1335 to the Bengal famine of 1943; the colonial-era set is structurally distinctive in its administrative response, but the underlying monsoon-and-state vulnerability is the longer story. Estimated 30–50 million dead across the six centuries.

collections.title: Land settlements of the Raj
collections.subtitle: Permanent Settlement, Ryotwari, Mahalwari — three colonial revenue systems, three rural class structures.
collections.summary: The EIC and Crown ran three distinct land-revenue systems across British India: Permanent Settlement (Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, 1793) with zamindars as proprietors and revenue fixed in perpetuity; Ryotwari (Madras, Bombay, from 1820) with the cultivator as direct revenue-payer; Mahalwari (North-Western Provinces, Punjab, from 1822) at the village joint-responsibility level. Each shaped the rural society of its region for two centuries.

collections.title: Bhakti and Sufi currents
collections.subtitle: Medieval devotional currents — Chishti silsila, Chaitanya's bhakti, Adi Shankara's monism — that re-shaped subcontinental religion across regions and confessions.
collections.summary: From Adi Shankara's eighth-century Advaita synthesis through Moinuddin Chishti's Sufi silsila at Ajmer (c. 1192), Nizamuddin Auliya's Chishti apex at Delhi, Chaitanya's Bengal Vaishnav movement (1510s), and the Bhakti poet-mystics — Kabir, Mirabai, Tukaram — the medieval devotional currents re-made subcontinental religious life. The Bhakti-Sufi vocabulary cut across Hindu-Muslim institutional religion and provided the cultural ground on which much modern Indian religious-political identity was later built.

collections.title: The Bengal Renaissance
collections.subtitle: Rammohan Roy to Vivekananda — the Calcutta-and-Bengali intellectual current of the colonial century.
collections.summary: From Rammohan Roy's Brahmo Sabha (1828) and the campaign against sati to Vivekananda's Chicago address (1893) and the Ramakrishna Mission (1897), the long Bengal Renaissance ran a religious-reformist, women's-rights, vernacular-literary, and pedagogical-modernist programme that re-shaped subcontinental intellectual life and provided much of the cultural ground on which Indian nationalism was built.

collections.title: The Indian scientific renaissance
collections.subtitle: J.C. Bose to Saha — the colonial-period generation that put India on the world scientific map.
collections.summary: Between 1885 and 1937 a generation of Indian scientists working in the colonial framework — J.C. Bose at Calcutta, Ramanujan at Cambridge under Hardy, C.V. Raman at IACS Calcutta, Meghnad Saha at UCL and Allahabad — produced first-rank original work in radio physics, number theory, light scattering, and astrophysics. Three of the four founded permanent Indian research institutions (Bose, Raman, Saha); Ramanujan's body of work continues to generate new mathematics a century after his death.

collections.title: The princely states question
collections.subtitle: From Doctrine of Lapse to integration — the 562 princely states between 1848 and 1948.
collections.summary: The princely states — 562 of them at Independence — were the unfinished business of British paramountcy. The Doctrine of Lapse annexed eight outright; the post-1858 Crown reasserted paramountcy on its own terms; integration after 1947 took two forms — Patel-Menon's Instruments of Accession for most, Operation Polo and Operation Vijay for Hyderabad and Goa, the unresolved Kashmir question for the remainder.
